First 30 Days in Finland: The Complete Expat Checklist

# First 30 Days in Finland: The Complete Expat Checklist

A week-by-week roadmap covering everything you need to set up in Finland in your first month — from HETU and bank account to tax card, Kela, Finnish ID

Compiled by Bikram Nath from the sources listed on this page

Who needs it

All new expats arriving in Finland — EU and non-EU

Week 1 priority

Register with DVV to get your henkilötunnus — bank, tax card, Kela, and Suomi.fi all require it

Tax card warning

Without a verokortti before your first paycheck, employer withholds 60% tax — order via OmaVero as soon as HETU is issued

Finnish ID card

Apply at DVV once you have a henkilötunnus and kotikunta — takes 2–4 weeks; apply in week 3–4

Watch out for

Kela coverage can start from day of move if residence is considered permanent or you earn ≥€800.02/month (2026 threshold)

14 min read· Verified 14 June 2026· [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] [6] [7]

Sources include dvv.fi, kela.fi and vero.fi. Last updated 23 October 2026; content last verified 14 June 2026.

Your first month in Finland is a chain of dependencies that mostly resolves itself once you understand the sequence. One task unlocks the next. Get out of order and you will spend time queuing at offices for things you could have done online, or watching an employer withhold 60% of your wages because a tax card was late. This guide maps the full 30 days — week by week — so you know exactly what to do and when.

If you have already landed and are in week 1, the granular day-by-day breakdown is in the first week in Finland checklist. This guide picks up where that leaves off and covers the full month, including the tasks that only become possible once your week-1 registration clears.

## Before You Arrive

Two things are worth doing before you board the flight.

Open a Wise account. Once you are in Finland, your salary will need somewhere to land before your Finnish bank account is open — and that can take 1–2 weeks after you arrive. A Wise multi-currency account gives you a real EU IBAN immediately, so your employer has an account to pay into from day one. You can also use it to convert money from home without the bank exchange-rate markup. Open it before you fly; verification takes a day or two.

Activate SafetyWing. Finnish public healthcare through Kela is excellent, but it does not start the moment you land. There is a processing lag between your DVV registration, your Kela application, and the point at which coverage is confirmed. SafetyWing's Nomad Insurance bridges that window — it covers emergency medical costs globally at a low monthly rate. It is the kind of thing you only miss when you need it. Activate it before you travel so there is no gap.

Book temporary housing for 4–6 weeks. Do not commit to a long-term lease before you arrive. You need to see the city, understand commute zones, and figure out which neighbourhoods work for your life. Short-term furnished rentals or serviced apartments give you that breathing room. A permanent address can come in week 2 or 3 once you have more information.

## Week 1: Registration — The Bottleneck That Controls Everything

Everything in Finland eventually traces back to your henkilötunnus — the Finnish personal identity code. Without it, you cannot open a Finnish bank account, get a tax card, register with Kela, or access most government digital services.

The henkilötunnus is issued by the DVV (Digi- ja väestötietovirasto, the Digital and Population Data Services Agency) when you register as a foreign national. There are two steps: submit the online foreigner registration form at dvv.fi, then attend an in-person appointment at a DVV service point.

The in-person appointment is the bottleneck. Wait times vary — in Helsinki they can stretch to a few weeks during busy periods. Book the appointment the day you land, even if you submit the form later.

For the full week-1 sequence — what documents to bring, what to expect at the DVV appointment, how to register your address, and what to do while you wait for the code to be processed — read the first week in Finland checklist. That guide covers days 1–7 in detail. This guide picks up from week 2 onwards, once your HETU is in hand.

The week-1 outcome you need: a henkilötunnus issued and confirmed by DVV, and your Finnish address registered with maistraatti. Without those two things, week 2 cannot start properly.

## Week 2: Bank Account, Pankkitunnukset, Kela, and SIM

Week 2 is the most action-heavy week of the month because the HETU unlocks several parallel tasks.

### Open a Finnish bank account

The three Finnish banks that are most straightforward for new arrivals are OP, Nordea, and Danske Bank. All three require:

- A valid passport or EU identity document
- Your henkilötunnus
- Proof of address (a rental contract or utility bill in your name)
- A reason for needing an account (employment contract or similar)

Book an in-person appointment — walk-ins are rarely accepted. Expect a wait of a few days to a week. During the appointment, the bank will also issue your pankkitunnukset (online banking credentials), which is a separate and critical item covered below.

Until your Finnish account is open, your Wise account handles salary receipts and card spending. Most Finnish retailers accept Visa and Mastercard, so you will not be stuck.

For a full comparison of Finnish banks for expats — including fees, English-language service, and which is fastest to open — read the best bank account for expats in Finland guide.

### Get pankkitunnukset — your key to Finnish digital government

Pankkitunnukset are the Finnish online banking login credentials used as a strong electronic identification method. In Finland, these credentials are not just for banking — they are how you log in to:

- OmaKela (Kela's self-service portal)
- OmaVero (tax administration portal at vero.fi)
- Suomi.fi (the national digital services hub)
- Most municipal and public authority portals

When you open your bank account, specifically ask the bank to set up online banking (verkkopankki) and issue you a code calculator or mobile authentication app. Without pankkitunnukset, you cannot complete weeks 3 and 4 of this checklist.

### Register with Kela

Once you have pankkitunnukset, log in to OmaKela at kela.fi and apply for coverage as someone moving to Finland for work. You will need:

- Your henkilötunnus
- Your pankkitunnukset for login
- Information about your employment (contract start date, employer)

If Kela confirms your residence qualifies, coverage can start from the date of your move. You will receive a Kelakortti (Kela health card) in the post within a few weeks. The card gives you access to prescription discounts at pharmacies and reimbursements for certain medical costs. Keep it once it arrives — pharmacists ask for it routinely.

### Get a Finnish SIM (if you have not already)

If you arrived on an eSIM or foreign roaming SIM from week 1, week 2 is the time to get a proper Finnish contract SIM. The main operators are DNA, Elisa, and Telia. Contract SIMs require identification and usually your henkilötunnus — another reason to do this after DVV registration. Contract plans are significantly cheaper than prepaid for data, which matters once you are using maps and streaming daily.

## Week 3: Tax Card, Health Centre Registration, and Siirto

### Get your tax card from OmaVero — do not miss this

The verokortti (tax card) is the most time-sensitive task in your entire first month. Finnish employers are required by law to withhold 60% tax on wages if no valid tax card is on file when payroll runs. That is not a temporary inconvenience — it can take months to recover overpaid withholding through a tax return.

Order your tax card through OmaVero at vero.fi. Log in with your pankkitunnukset. You will be asked to estimate your annual income for the year. Based on that estimate, Vero calculates your withholding percentage. The tax card is then either downloaded directly or sent electronically to your employer.

Do this in week 3 at the latest, before your first payday. If your first payday falls in week 3 or 4, do it immediately in week 2. The OmaVero guide for foreigners walks through the full process step by step — see the OmaVero guide for foreigners.

### Register at your local terveyskeskus

Once you are registered with Kela and have a confirmed municipality of residence, register at your local terveyskeskus (municipal health centre). You do not have to visit in an emergency — registration is the step that assigns you a home health centre, which you then contact for non-emergency GP appointments.

Your terveyskeskus is determined by your registered address. Find yours through your municipality's website or via infofinland.fi. Registration is usually done online or by phone. Without it, you pay a higher fee for appointments and may be redirected to a different centre.

For a full explanation of how the Finnish public health system is structured — tiers, referrals, private vs. public, prescription costs — read the Finnish healthcare system explained guide.

### Set up Siirto

Siirto is Finland's peer-to-peer instant payment network, similar to Swish in Sweden or MobilePay in Denmark. It is embedded in most Finnish bank apps and lets you send money instantly using just a Finnish phone number. Most Finnish colleagues, landlords, and friends paying shared bills will use Siirto.

Enable it through your bank's mobile app. You link your Finnish phone number to your account, and transfers arrive within seconds. It requires your Finnish bank account and Finnish SIM — both of which you now have.

## Week 4: Finnish ID Card, Suomi.fi, and Tax Card Review

### Apply for your Finnish identity card

A Finnish henkilökortti (identity card) is not strictly required — you can use your passport or EU ID card indefinitely — but it is a practical document to have. It is accepted as ID everywhere in Finland, fits in a wallet, is cheaper to replace than a passport, and is the credential some government services prefer for strong identification.

Apply in person at a DVV service point. Processing takes 2–4 weeks, which is why you apply in week 4 rather than waiting. The card will arrive within your first two months if you apply now.

What you need:

- Your passport or current EU identity card
- Your henkilötunnus
- A confirmed municipality of residence registered with DVV
- The application fee (check the current amount at dvv.fi — fees are updated periodically)

Children under 15 need a guardian present. There is no minimum age requirement.

### Set up Suomi.fi

Suomi.fi is Finland's national digital services portal. Once set up, it lets you:

- Access official government services with a single login
- Grant authorisations (for example, letting someone manage government services on your behalf)
- Receive official Finnish correspondence digitally rather than by post
- Manage information across multiple public authorities

Log in at suomi.fi using your pankkitunnukset. The setup itself takes under 10 minutes. Enabling digital post delivery is the first thing worth doing once you are logged in — it means official letters from Kela, Vero, and DVV arrive in the portal rather than at your address, which matters if you move or are not always home.

### Review your verokortti

Your tax card estimate from week 3 was based on projected annual income. If anything has changed — different salary, bonus structure, second income — log back in to OmaVero and update the estimate. Vero recalculates the withholding percentage and sends an updated card to your employer automatically.

This is also the time to read the Finnish tax system explained guide if you have not already. Finland's progressive tax rates, the municipal tax component, and the mechanics of year-end tax returns are worth understanding before your first full year of filing.

## Common Problems and Fixes

Strong identification in Finland 2026: personal code and bank codes | Selkoraha

# Strong identification in Finland 2026: personal code and bank codes

Published 16 July 2026 · Updated 29 October 2026 · Author: Palvemax OY

Using Finnish e-services requires two things: a personal identity code (henkilötunnus) and strong electronic identification. Strong identification is most often done with online banking codes, a mobile certificate or a certificate card, and through the Suomi.fi service you log into Kela, Vero, Migri (Enter Finland) and OmaKanta with them.

If you do not yet have a Finnish personal identity code or bank codes, you can use another EU country’s eIDAS token or the Finnish Authenticator app. Below is where to get the personal code, what strong-identification methods exist and how to get around the chicken-and-egg problem.

11

## What is the personal identity code and where do you get it?

The personal identity code (henkilötunnus) is 11 characters long, the first six formed from your date of birth. It is issued when your data is registered in the Population Information System. If you are granted a residence permit or a registered right of residence by Migri, the code is usually created automatically and printed on the residence permit card.

Otherwise you request it from the Digital and Population Data Services Agency (DVV): you fill in an online form and visit in person within a month. Processing typically takes about 2–4 weeks. For the visit you need a valid passport or EU ID card and a residence permit card or other proof of legal residence. You need the code at a bank, with an employer and in dealings with authorities.

## Strong electronic identification – bank codes and other methods

With Suomi.fi e-Identification you log into public-administration services with a single sign-in. The strong-identification methods are online banking codes, a mobile certificate and a certificate card (such as the ID card issued by the police). You get online banking codes by making a contract with a Finnish bank, and they must be issued to you personally. A mobile certificate is activated with your operator and often requires existing bank codes – it does not work on a prepaid subscription.

## The chicken-and-egg problem: what without a code or an account?

Bank codes require a bank account, and opening an account requires a personal identity code and strong identification – often a visit to a branch. So in practice the first strong token is usually the online banking codes. If you cannot get a Finnish token yet, you can use your own EU country’s eIDAS token or the Finnish Authenticator app (for people without a personal code, 18+, in English) – though it does not work in every service.

A fintech account (such as Revolut or Wise) helps at the first stage with salary and payments, but it does not give Finnish strong identification to Kela, Vero or Migri. It is a good bridge while you wait, not a replacement for a Finnish bank and bank codes.

Strong-identification methods in Finland 2026

| Method | For whom | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Online banking codes | Customer of a Finnish bank | Most common; needs a bank account |
| Mobile certificate | Operator subscription | Not on prepaid; activation often via bank codes |
| Certificate card / ID card | Issued by the police | High assurance level |
| Finnish Authenticator | Without a personal code (18+) | In English; not in every service |
| eIDAS token | Another EU country’s token | Works in Finnish authority e-services |

## For entrepreneurs: you need the codes for company matters too

You also need strong identification when you start a business. A limited company’s start-up notification is filed online in the YTJ service, which you log into with Suomi.fi e-Identification. Logging in requires a Finnish personal identity code and a Finnish means of identification. If you do not have them yet, PRH says an authorised contact person or an attorney can file the notification. A sole trader can also start the business in MyTax (OmaVero), using the same credentials.

A business account can be opened online too. The payment institution Holvi, for example, identifies you with Finnish online banking codes or a mobile certificate. A bank has no duty to open an account for a company, so we have written separately about where to get a business account if a bank will not open one.

## FAQ

Where do I get a Finnish personal identity code?+

It is created when your data is registered in the Population Information System. With a Migri residence permit usually automatically (shown on the permit card); otherwise you request it from DVV via an online form and a visit, processing about 2–4 weeks.

What strong-identification methods are there?+

Online banking codes, a mobile certificate and a certificate card (such as the police-issued ID card). Through Suomi.fi you log into public-administration services with them.

How do I identify myself without a Finnish personal code?+

You can use your own EU country’s eIDAS token or the Finnish Authenticator app (for people aged 18+, in English). However, not every service accepts the latter.

Is Revolut or Wise enough for strong identification?+

No. A fintech account helps with salary and payments, but it does not give Finnish strong identification to Kela, Vero or Migri. For that you need a Finnish bank’s codes, a mobile certificate or a certificate card.

Can I get bank codes without a bank account?+

No. Online banking codes are issued together with a bank account under a contract. Opening an account in turn requires a personal identity code and proof of identity.

Your Complete First 30 Days in Finland — Checklist and Guide — FinMigrants

# Your Complete First 30 Days in Finland — Checklist and Guide

FI

 FinMigrants 

· April 10, 2026 Updated April 28, 2026

 

Your first month in Finland is the most admin-heavy period you will ever face here. Doing things in the wrong order can set you back weeks. This is the checklist we wish we had when we landed.

## Before You Land

- Book a DVV appointment before you arrive — they fill up 2-4 weeks in advance.
- Ensure your residence permit or EU right of residence is in order.
- Download the official Suomi.fi app.
- Get a European Health Insurance Card if you are an EU/EEA citizen.

## Week 1: Registration First

Everything else depends on your henkilotunnus. Go to DVV (Digi- ja vaestotietovirasto) as soon as possible. Bring your passport, lease agreement, and residence permit if applicable. You will typically receive your henkilotunnus on the same day or within a few days by post.

## Week 1-2: Bank Account

Open a bank account as soon as you have your henkilotunnus. S-Pankki is usually the most accessible for newcomers. Visit a branch with your passport and henkilotunnus.

## Week 2: Kela Registration

Kela is Finland Social Insurance Institution. Register at kela.fi and apply for the general housing allowance if your rent and income qualify. Students can apply for the student grant (opintoraha).

## Week 3-4: Tax Card

Before you can work in Finland, you need a tax card (verokortti). Get it at vero.fi — it is free and takes about 10 minutes online. Send the tax card to your employer immediately — without it, they will withhold tax at 60%.

> By end of week 4 you should have: henkilotunnus, Finnish bank account, Kela registration, Finnish SIM card, tax card, and Finnish eID active.

sources.title: Best Bank Accounts in Finland for Expats (2026) | NordicExpat
highlights:
Suomi.fi confirms that online banking codes are accepted as strong electronic identification across services well beyond the bank itself.

...

- Which English-speaking branch can see you soonest? Because the first account is opened in person, appointment availability often matters more than the brand. Nordea and OP have the widest reach here.
- Do you already collect a loyalty scheme? If you shop at S-Group, S-Pankki's bonuses fold neatly into spending you already do. If you expect to use one provider for insurance and a mortgage too, OP's member model rewards consolidation.
- How much do you need English self-service? If you will not read Finnish for a while, weight English online banking heavily — this is where the smaller banks fall short.
- How fast do you need the online banking codes? Remember the account and the codes are separate. If getting your pankkitunnukset quickly is the priority (to file taxes or access Kela online), ask the bank directly about the codes, not just the account, at your appointment.

...

Once your account is open, the codes are the prize. As Suomi.fi explains, online banking codes must be issued personally to you and are obtained by entering into a contract with a Finnish bank.

...

A few things to know:

- They are not automatic with the account. Especially for newcomers, the strong-identification step can lag behind account opening — the exact gap the FIN-FSA review flagged. Ask at your appointment specifically when and how you will receive your codes.
- There are alternatives. Finland also recognises the mobile certificate (mobiilivarmenne, a chip-based identity tied to your SIM, offered by mobile operators), certificate cards, and the Finnish Authenticator app. If bank codes are slow, mobiilivarmenne can be a useful second route into Suomi.fi services.
- Joint accounts have a quirk. Per Suomi.fi, online banking codes for a joint account can be used only by the person in whose name the account is held — so each adult generally needs their own codes.

...

Done in this order, you avoid the most common failure mode: assuming the account and the codes arrive together, and being stuck unable to log in to public services for weeks. For the step-by-step mechanics of the visit itself, see our guide to opening a bank account in Finland; for the codes specifically, see our guide to Finnish online banking IDs.

It is operated by the Digital and Population Data Services Agency (Finnish Digi- ja väestötietovirasto · Swedish Myndigheten för digitalisering och befolkningsdata, "DVV"). Newcomers usually enrol through Mobiilivarmenne · Mobilcertifikat (Mobile Certificate) issued by one of the three Finnish mobile operators, online banking codes from a Finnish bank, or the Citizen Certificate smartcard on the police-issued identity card.

Estimated time

Mobile Certificate activation is same-session — the credential is usable within minutes of bank-credential authentication at the operator portal. Online banking credentials are issued through the bank's own onboarding window, typically alongside account opening. The Citizen Certificate route takes longer because the activation code travels by post after the police-issued identity card is picked up; the postal step alone is up to two weeks. Cross-border foreign electronic identifiers register immediately on first sign-in, with no separate enrolment inside Finland.

The bank issues the online banking codes after completing its own customer-identification flow against the Finnish personal identity code.
2. (Applicant) At a Suomi.fi-tunnistus picker, select the bank's icon. The picker redirects to the bank's own authentication flow; the customer completes the bank's strong-authentication step and is returned to the destination e-service.
3. (Bank) Vouches for the identification event to the destination e-service over the Suomi.fi-tunnistus gateway.

💡 Tip: The online-banking-codes route does not require any additional enrolment beyond holding usable codes at the bank. The same codes are also the bootstrap identifier used when activating Mobile Certificate.

3. (Applicant) Install the agency's chip-card reader software on a computer and connect a chip-card reader. Run the activation flow, enter the posted activation code, and set two personal codes — one used for identification and one used for electronic signatures.

...

- → Activate the everyday e-services you will use first — MyTax for tax matters, OmaKela for social-security and health-insurance matters, the Migri visa-portal for immigration matters, and the Suomi.fi web service itself for messages and authority correspondence.
- → If you have already received the Finnish identity card with the chip, plan the Citizen Certificate activation early — the postal activation code can take up to two weeks, and the chip-card reader and reader software need to be set up before the first sign-in.
- → If you change Finnish mobile operator, re-enrol Mobile Certificate with the new operator — the credential is bound to the SIM, not portable across operators.
- → If you hold a foreign electronic identifier notified under the EU electronic-identity scheme, check before each new destination e-service whether that service accepts foreign electronic identifiers.

sources.title: Finnish Online Banking IDs (Pankkitunnukset) | NordicExpat
highlights:
### 3. Confirm the codes are identification-enabled

When you become a customer you typically receive an account, online access codes and a debit card together. Ask the bank explicitly that your codes are enabled for strong electronic identification, not only for banking. Suomi.fi stresses that, to be valid for e-identification, the codes must be "suitable for electronic identification in other services in addition to banking transactions," and they must have been issued personally to you — company or association codes do not count, and on a joint account only the named account holder can use them.

### 4. If you lack accepted documents

This is the hard case that catches many non-EU arrivals. If you do not have an ID document the bank accepts, you may not be able to activate e-identification straight away. Nordea describes a workaround used in Finland: you can visit a police station, where your identity is verified so the electronic identification service can be activated. Banks also commonly send an activation code and a temporary PIN by SMS and by post as part of setting up their identification app.

Because rules and accepted documents vary between banks and change over time, confirm the current requirements with your chosen bank before you go in.

...

Modern Finnish banking codes almost always involve an app on your phone for the confirmation step rather than a paper code list. Setup usually means installing the bank's identification app, registering it once, and choosing a PIN. After that, logging in to any Suomi.fi-connected service follows the same rhythm: choose your bank, enter your user ID and password, then approve the login in the app or with a one-time code.

A few habits keep this smooth:

- Keep your phone and SIM working. App-based confirmation depends on your device; a lost or wiped phone means re-registering the app with your bank.
- Don't rely on a single method. Many residents also activate a mobile certificate as a backup, so a phone problem doesn't lock them out of tax or healthcare.
- Mind the personal-use rule. Never let anyone else use your codes, even a spouse on a joint account — it breaks both the bank's terms and the identification rules.

...

## Common Problems and How to Avoid Them

A few situations recur often enough to flag:

- "I have an account but can't log in to OmaVero." Your codes are probably not activated for e-identification. Call the bank and ask them to enable identification use.
- A lost or new phone. Re-register the bank's identification app, or fall back to a mobile certificate if you set one up. Plan for this before it happens.
- Forgotten codes. Suomi.fi's guidance is simple: if you don't remember your online banking codes, contact your bank — neither Suomi.fi nor the public service can recover them.
- Sharing codes. Letting a family member log in "just this once" with your codes breaches the personal-use rule and can put your bank relationship at risk.

sources.title: Bank account in Finland – online banking codes
highlights:
In Finland the bank account and the online banking codes (verkkopankkitunnukset) that come with it are two different things. The codes are the everyday electronic identity: they log you in to Suomi.fi e-Identification, the shared login for public e-services, and so to Kela (Social Insurance Institution), Vero (Tax Administration) and the police. Opening a bank account in Finland is a legal right for anyone legally resident in the EEA, and strong identification can be refused only on narrow grounds. The rules are national, set in the Act on Credit Institutions and supervised by the Financial Supervisory Authority (Finanssivalvonta).

...

Because the law treats them separately. The requirements for online banking credentials are stricter than for the account, so some newcomers leave the branch with an account and no codes. A bank may refuse strong electronic identification – codes that work in other services, not only its own – if, for example, you have no Finnish personal identity code or are not in the Population Information System. It must then offer a limited electronic ID for its own services; once your code and registration are in place, ask again. Codes used for Suomi.fi must be issued personally to you and be suitable for other services.

Take phishing seriously: the Financial Supervisory Authority calls the fishing of online banking codes the most common scam in Finland. No bank or authority ever asks for your codes by phone or e-mail, so never log in through a link in a message, and never let anyone take remote control of your device.

...

Suomi.fi e-Identification is free for private individuals and accepts several tokens.

| Token | Who can use it | What you need |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Finnish online banking codes | Bank customers with a personal identity code | Personal codes suitable for other services |
| Mobile certificate (mobiilivarmenne) | Customers of DNA, Elisa or Telia | Finnish online banking codes to activate it; not on a prepaid subscription |
| Finnish ID card with citizen certificate | Finnish citizens; foreigners permanently resident with a valid permit or registered right of residence | Activate the certificate, then use the mobile app or a card reader with DVV's free software |
| Tokens of 21 other European countries (eIDAS) | Citizens of, for example, Estonia, Germany, Sweden and Spain | Only in e-services that allow foreign users |
| Finnish Authenticator app | Foreigners aged 18 or over with no Finnish code or token | A passport or EU, EEA, UK or Swiss ID card to photograph; not strong identification |

...

## What to do now

| Step | What | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Get your henkilötunnus and DVV registration (part 3) | Before you book the bank |
| 2 | Book an in-person appointment; bring your passport or foreigner's ID card | Your first week |
| 3 | Answer the know-your-customer questions; ask for codes usable in other services | At the appointment |
| 4 | If refused: ask for the reason in writing and a limited e-ID | When the bank answers – at most ten banking days |
| 5 | Apply for the foreigner's ID card as a second token (€53 online) | Once you have a kotikunta |
| 6 | Activate a mobile certificate, then MobilePay | When the codes work |

Source: the Financial Supervisory Authority, the Finnish Police and Suomi.fi, read 24 September 2026.

sources.title: Digital ID in Finland: bank codes and the new wallet | Hello Expat
highlights:
The usual methods are:

- Bank codes (pankkitunnukset): the codes your Finnish bank gives you under a contract. They must be personal and enabled for electronic identification; business codes do not count.
- Mobile certificate (mobiilivarmenne): a certificate on the SIM card of a DNA, Elisa or Telia subscription, activated with your bank codes. It does not work on a prepaid card; for an eSIM, ask the operator.
- Police identity card: foreign residents who live in Finland permanently, are in the population register, have a registered right of residence and a municipality of residence can apply for a police-issued identity card. You activate its certificate and use it with a card reader or the hightrust.id app.
- hightrust.id: a free wallet app that can be activated with a police identity card issued after 31 August 2021, including the residence card for foreigners.

...

Not much, and that is the awkward part. Before you have a personal identity code, you cannot get bank codes. Before you have bank codes, you cannot get the mobile certificate. See the Finnish personal identity code and opening a bank account in Finland for the first two steps.

For the gap, there is Finnish Authenticator, a free app for foreigners who have no Finnish identification. You create a foreigner identifier with your email, then prove your identity in the app by photographing your passport, or your national identity card if you are a citizen of the EU, the EEA, Switzerland or the UK, and taking a selfie. A driving licence is not accepted.

Two cautions. Each service decides whether it accepts Finnish Authenticator. Vero says that OmaVero accepts personal bank codes, the mobile certificate, certificate cards and hightrust.id, and that Finnish Authenticator is there for foreign company representatives with a Suomi.fi authorisation. Private persons from another EU country can use their own eIDAS identity for a limited set of functions. And the account is blocked if unused for four years.

...

Because the conditions are stricter. A foreigner can sometimes hold an account yet not receive codes. Under Finnish law a bank may refuse codes only where you do not have a personal identity code or are not registered in the population register, and it must then offer you a limited identification method for use of the account. Ask the bank in writing if you are refused.

Your bank codes also work as an electronic signature. Never lend them, not even to a partner. A joint account's codes serve only the holder to whom they were issued.

...

## How do you get your digital ID in Finland in practice?

1. Get your identity code and a municipality of residence.
2. Open a bank account and ask explicitly for online banking codes.
3. Activate a mobile certificate on a subscription, not a prepaid card.
4. Once you qualify, apply for the police identity card for foreigners and activate its certificate.
5. Keep two different methods. Losing your phone or changing your bank can lock you out of OmaVero and OmaKela.

...

## How do you avoid scams around digital ID?

The Tax Administration warns on its own website that scam messages have been sent in its name, and similar messages circulate in the name of Kela and banks. The rule is the same as anywhere: do not click a link in a message, open the service by typing the address or using the official app, and never read out an authorisation code to a caller. If you lose your phone, call your bank's helpline at once to block your codes.

## Which mistakes do newcomers make?

Counting on a French or other national eID without checking the list. Buying a prepaid SIM and expecting a mobile certificate. Believing every service accepts Finnish Authenticator. Letting the app account sleep. And lending codes, which is both unwise and against the bank's terms.

sources.title: Strong Identification Finland: EUR 53 ID Card Option | ENB
highlights:
The identity code is a population identifier; bank credentials, mobile certificates and certificate cards are separately issued authentication tools.

...

Suomi.fi's 2026 guidance lists personal Finnish online banking credentials, mobile certificates from DNA/Elisa/Telia, police-issued certificate cards, Hightrust.id and supported foreign identification methods among the available tokens. The e-service uses Suomi.fi to verify the selected method.

...

## 4. A bank account and strong bank identification are not the same service

A Finnish bank can provide a payment account while strong personal banking credentials suitable for e-identification remain subject to separate conditions. Suomi.fi states that banking credentials used for electronic identification must be issued personally to you and enabled for identification in services beyond ordinary banking transactions.

Access to a joint account or company online banking does not automatically create personal strong identification. Ask the bank specifically whether the credentials are enabled for strong electronic identification in external services.

...

Bank user IDs, passwords, code lists, mobile-certificate PINs and authentication approvals are personal. If a consultant, accountant, employer or family member needs to act on your behalf, use a lawful authorisation mechanism rather than sharing authentication credentials.
